estimation.summary: Turn vague requirements into numbers you can design against: request rates, storage, bandwidth, concurrency and availability. Getting within a factor of two is the goal; a dropped zero is the real risk.
points: A day has 86,400 seconds (about 10^5), so 1M requests/day is about 12 QPS on average. Multiply by a peak factor (often 2-5×) and leave headroom on top.
Storage = items/day × bytes/item × retention × replication factor. Write out the units at every step.
Bandwidth is quoted in bits and storage in bytes. 1 MB/s = 8 Mbps, so mixing them is an 8× error.
Little's Law: in-flight requests = arrival rate × average time in the system (L = λW). Use it to size thread pools, connection pools and worker counts.
Know the latency ladder: RAM about 100 ns, same-datacenter round trip about 0.5 ms, disk seek about 10 ms, intercontinental round trip about 150 ms.
Availability: serial dependencies multiply their availabilities, while redundant replicas multiply their unavailabilities. Fan-out turns a leaf's rare p99 into the common case: 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 63%.
traps: Sizing for the daily average instead of the peak hour.
Assuming redundant replicas fail independently, when shared deploys, configs and zones make them fail together.
Averaging latencies by hit ratio the wrong way round: at an 80% hit ratio, the database still dominates the mean.

scaling-basics.summary: Scale out by making instances interchangeable, routing work to them with the right balancing policy, and watching the real saturation signal. Know where adding machines stops helping.
points: Vertical scaling (a bigger box) is simple but has a ceiling and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (more boxes) needs stateless instances or partitioned state.
Keep request-handling tiers stateless: put sessions in a shared store or in signed client tokens so any instance can serve any request.
A layer-4 balancer works per TCP connection. A layer-7 balancer works per request, can route by path or header, and must terminate TLS to do so.
Round robin assumes equal-cost requests. Least-outstanding-requests or power-of-two-choices handle variable costs, and power of two is robust to stale load information.
Modulo hashing remaps about N/(N+1) of keys when a node is added. Consistent hashing remaps only about 1/(N+1).
Scale on the resource that actually saturates. An I/O-bound tier needs concurrency or latency signals, not CPU, and scaling it out can overload the database behind it.
traps: Treating sticky sessions as a scaling strategy: state still dies with the instance.
Expecting more nodes to always add throughput. Cross-node coordination (the coherency cost) can make throughput fall.
Terminating instances without draining them first, which drops in-flight requests on every deploy.
